newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish c.bank ups reverse repo rate to curb credit.
newsitem.headline: Polish c.bank ups reverse repo rate to curb credit.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland (NBP) raised its maximum reverse repo rate on Thursday for the second time in a row in what analysts said was yet another measure to curb too fast credit growth.

From January to March 10 credit for the non-financial sector rose 6.5 percent while non-financial sector deposits rose 2.2 percent. In the same period last year credit rose 3.9 percent while deposits rose 7.4 percent.
In nominal terms credit since the start of the year to March 10 grew 5.22 billion zlotys to 86.14 billion while deposits grew 1.93 billion zlotys to 90.87 billion.
"The NBP is raising market rates to cool down the economy by curbing credit action and...diminish the worrying trade gap," said Pawel Krawczykiewicz, analyst at PBI SA.
On Thursday the NBP raised the maximum 14-day reverse repo rate to 22.15 percent from 21.65 percent last week.
"The bank is likely to have acted on early data on credit growth and current account," Krawczykiewicz said.

To curb fast credit growth the NBP has already raised from the start of March the obligatory reserve requirements for banks for zloty call deposits by three points to 20 percent and all currency deposits by two points to four percent.

The central bank has been concerned that the fast growth of credit boosts imports, which in January were 41 percent higher than a year ago while exports were only 9.7 percent higher than in January 1996.
In the whole of 1996 exports rose 6.7 percent while imports rose 31 percent as credit rose more than 40 percent.
"To keep up exports the NBP is influencing the short end of the yield curve while keeping the zloty anchored," said Rafal Petsch of Bank of America in London.

The central bank has repeatedly stepped in to stop the zloty's rise at three percent from the centre of the 14-percent trading band. The last, symbolically small dollar-buying intervention of $4 million was on Wednedsay.
"The NBP is raising market rates and at the same time keeping a lid on the zloty because a stronger Polish currency would offset the effect of higher rates," Petsch said.
Poland's current account gap in January rose to $899 million from $368 million in December and $139 million in January 1996.

It was $1.35 billion zlotys for the whole of 1996 against a $5.46 billion surplus in 1995 or 0.75 percent of the gross domestic product. The finance ministry expect the current account gap might rise to between three and 3.5 percent of GDP this year.
